Adapting DietView to your own survey

Source: vignettes/articles/extending.Rmd
extending.Rmd

DietView makes few assumptions about your data: one row per prey record, a predator column, a stomach column and a prey key. Everything else is declared. This article goes through the choices you make when you bring a survey of your own, in the order you meet them. The worked example is the public ICES stomach data that ship with the package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see ?ices_diet): a real survey export, with its own column names and codes, that was not designed for DietView.

library(DietView)

1. Map your columns

Start from the table as you have it. ices_diet keeps the column names of the stomachr extract:

names(ices_diet)
#>  [1] "stomach_id"        "prey_aphia_id"     "prey_name"        
#>  [4] "item_type"         "digestion_stage"   "digestion_label"  
#>  [7] "prey_count"        "prey_weight_g"     "prey_length_cm"   
#> [10] "haul_id"           "country"           "survey"           
#> [13] "year"              "month"             "quarter"          
#> [16] "lat"               "lon"               "ices_rectangle"   
#> [19] "depth_m"           "region"            "predator_aphia_id"
#> [22] "predator_latin"    "predator_common"   "n_fish_pooled"    
#> [25] "length_cm"         "weight_g"          "stomach_empty"    
#> [28] "regurgitated"

Then decide which column plays which role. Your table keeps its own column names; dv_spec() only records the mapping:

Role ICES column Note
predator predator_common a display label; predator_aphia_id or predator_latin would do as well
predator_latin predator_latin used for the species cards
stomach stomach_id must be unique across the whole table
prey_id prey_aphia_id the WoRMS AphiaID, NA for unidentified material
prey_name prey_name the scientific name, used when there is no ID
weight prey_weight_g grams
count prey_count individuals per record, for %N
digestion digestion_stage or a label built from it see below
covariates region, year, quarter, … anything you will compare across

Survey exports usually need a few decisions before the mapping is complete. The ICES data need four.

The stomach identifier. It must be unique across the whole table, not only within a predator, a haul or a year: stomach counts (frequency of occurrence, aggregation thresholds, matrices) count distinct identifiers, so two stomachs that share an identifier count as one. Check it:

pred_per_stomach <- tapply(ices_diet$predator_common, ices_diet$stomach_id,
                           function(z) length(unique(z)))
table(pred_per_stomach)
#> pred_per_stomach
#>    1 
#> 4231
hauls_per_stomach <- tapply(ices_diet$haul_id, ices_diet$stomach_id,
                            function(z) length(unique(z)))
table(hauls_per_stomach)
#> hauls_per_stomach
#>    1 
#> 4231

Each ICES stomach belongs to one predator and one haul. If your identifiers restart in each haul or each year, build a unique one first, for example mydata$stom <- paste(mydata$haul_id, mydata$fish_no, sep = "_"). A related case: 7 stomach samples in ices_diet pool two fish (n_fish_pooled == 2). They are one identifier and are counted as one stomach; say so, or drop them.

What counts as diet. The export lists everything found in the stomach:

table(ices_diet$item_type)
#> 
#>     non_food         prey unidentified 
#>           67         8019         1553
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
sum(phylum %in% "Nematoda")
#> [1] 1042

Non-food items (sand, stones, plastic) are not diet. Nematodes in fish stomachs are mostly parasites. Unidentified material is diet whose taxon is unknown, and it stays. DietView does not filter for you; the documentation drops the first two:

dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

Digestion codes. ICES reports the digestion stage as a code (0, 1, 2), missing for many records. You can declare the code column directly (digestion = "digestion_stage"), but the missing stages then appear as an NA group in dv_digestion_diagnostic(), easy to confuse with unidentified prey, and a bare code is hard to read in a table. The bundled data carry a label column built like this:

lab <- c("0" = "0 pristine", "1" = "1 affected", "2" = "2 skeletal remains")
dl  <- unname(lab[as.character(dat$digestion_stage)])
dl[is.na(dl)] <- "not recorded"
identical(dl, dat$digestion_label)
#> [1] TRUE
table(dl)
#> dl
#>         0 pristine         1 affected 2 skeletal remains       not recorded 
#>                561               3494               2206               2269

The labels are inferred from the older ICES format, whose three classes match the shares of codes 0, 1 and 2; check them against the ICES vocabulary before you rely on them. “not recorded” keeps the records without a stage in the table as a group of their own.

Units. Check them before anything else, against the survey documentation and against the values. When the bundled data were built, two unit errors in the predator variables were fixed (Belgian lengths reported in mm, Danish weights in kg). A quick look at the range of each numeric column per country catches most of them:

round(sapply(split(dat$length_cm, dat$country), max, na.rm = TRUE))
#>  BE  DE  DK  NL  NO  SE 
#>  35  85 104  95  57  97

With those decisions made, declare and validate:

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)
dv_validate(dat, spec)
#> 8530 records from 4222 stomachs of 22 predator(s); 2305 stomach(s) hold a single record; 531 record(s) lack a weight.

Give both a prey ID and a prey name when you have them: the ID is used for the lookup, and the name lets DietView check that the two agree. In the ICES data every identified prey has an AphiaID; the 1,553 records without one are the unidentified material.

2. Attach a taxonomy you can check

With taxonomy = "worms", DietView looks each distinct prey up in the World Register of Marine Species and keeps a log of how it was matched. Read that log before you use the result:

prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms")
dv_taxonomy_report(prep)   # the matches that need a look, largest first

For the ICES data that means 252 lookups by AphiaID, plus one by name for “Unidentified material”, which is expected to stay unresolved. Each prey gets a match_type:

match_type Meaning What to do
id The AphiaID is accepted in WoRMS Nothing, unless name_check is "differs"
id_synonym The AphiaID is unaccepted; its accepted ID was used Check that the accepted name is the taxon you meant
id_unchecked WoRMS could not be reached to check the ID Run again later
exact No ID; the name matched exactly Nothing
fuzzy No ID; the name was matched by TAXAMATCH, which tolerates misspellings Check every one: a near match can be a different taxon
unresolved No match Correct the name, or accept that the prey stays unidentified

A name_check of "differs" means the name in your table is not the name WoRMS holds for that AphiaID: either the ID or the name was mistyped. A lineage_ok of FALSE means the prey was matched but its classification could not be retrieved; its records count as unidentified until you run the lookup again. Fix what the report lists, then save the lineage.

3. Freeze the taxonomy for the analysis

WoRMS changes. For an analysis you will publish, resolve the taxonomy once, save it as a lineage table, and run every later step from that file. ices_lineage is such a table:

dim(ices_lineage)
#> [1] 461  10
ices_lineage[ices_lineage$scientific_name %in% c("Crangon crangon", "Crustacea", "Pisces"), ]
#>    prey_aphia_id scientific_name worms_rank  kingdom     phylum        class
#> 48        107552 Crangon crangon    Species Animalia Arthropoda Malacostraca
#> 77          1066       Crustacea  Subphylum Animalia Arthropoda         <NA>
#> 81         11676          Pisces Superclass Animalia   Chordata         <NA>
#>       order      family   genus         species
#> 48 Decapoda Crangonidae Crangon Crangon crangon
#> 77     <NA>        <NA>    <NA>            <NA>
#> 81     <NA>        <NA>    <NA>            <NA>

It has one row per AphiaID, a key column named like the prey_id column of the data (prey_aphia_id), and one column per rank; an empty cell means the prey was not identified to that rank. scientific_name and worms_rank are kept for the reader and ignored by DietView.

Freezing your own takes two lines after a WoRMS run, and the frozen table gives exactly the same result offline. Here, starting from a prepared object:

prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)

keep <- !is.na(prep$data$prey_aphia_id)
lineage <- unique(prep$data[keep, c("prey_aphia_id", prep$ranks)])
nrow(lineage)
#> [1] 252

f <- file.path(tempdir(), "lineage_2026-10-20.csv")
write.csv(lineage, f, row.names = FALSE)

lineage2 <- read.csv(f, na.strings = c("NA", ""))
prep2 <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lineage2,
                    verbose = FALSE)
identical(dv_tree(prep), dv_tree(prep2))
#> [1] TRUE

This path needs neither worrms nor a network connection, and it gives the same result every time it is run on the same files. Archive the lineage table with your data and record the date it was retrieved. A prey that is missing from the lineage table, or a key that appears twice, triggers a warning or an error instead of passing unnoticed:

crangon <- ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id[ices_lineage$scientific_name == "Crangon crangon"]
prep3 <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table",
                    lineage = lineage2[lineage2$prey_aphia_id != crangon, ],
                    verbose = FALSE)
#> Warning: 1 prey key(s) are absent from `lineage` (e.g. 107552); their records
#> are treated as fully unidentified.

If you build the lineage table by hand, for example for prey outside WoRMS, take the classification from one stated authority and cite it.

4. Choose the ranks

By default DietView shows seven ranks, kingdom to species. Pass ranks to show others; every rank you list must be a column of the lineage table:

spec5 <- dv_spec(predator = "predator_common", stomach = "stomach_id",
                 prey_id = "prey_aphia_id", prey_name = "prey_name",
                 weight = "prey_weight_g",
                 ranks = c("phylum", "class", "order", "family", "genus"))
prep5 <- dv_prepare(dat, spec5, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                    verbose = FALSE)
c(seven_ranks = nrow(dv_tree(prep)), five_ranks = nrow(dv_tree(prep5)))
#> seven_ranks  five_ranks 
#>         702         458

Rank names are WoRMS rank names in lower case, so on the WoRMS path intermediate ranks such as "subclass" or "infraorder" can be added. A frozen table holds only the ranks it was built with: ices_lineage has the seven default ones, so adding "infraorder" (which would separate crabs from shrimps inside Decapoda) means going back to WoRMS once and freezing again.

Fewer ranks make a simpler figure, but they also merge information: without "species", a prey named to species and one named only to its genus look the same. Check one more thing on your own prey list: some taxa have no entry at one of the requested ranks in WoRMS. Such a prey shows an unidentified node at that rank with named taxa beyond it, and that node then mixes prey that were not identified with prey that were identified but have no taxon at that rank. Find those nodes before you report an unidentified share:

tree <- dv_tree(prep)
named_kids <- tapply(tree$label != "NA", tree$parent, any)
holes <- tree[tree$label == "NA" & tree$id %in% names(named_kids)[named_kids], ]
holes[, c("id", "rank", "value_occ")]
#>                                  id  rank value_occ
#> 45           Animalia|Priapulida|NA Class         7
#> 55  Animalia|Annelida|Polychaeta|NA Order       470
#> 69 Animalia|Chordata|Leptocardii|NA Order         1

In the ICES data these are the polychaetes, whose unidentified order node holds 470 records, some of them in families that WoRMS places in no order; a lancelet (Leptocardii) with a family but no order; and Priapulida, which have no class. Their NA rows in dv_rank_table() at that rank are not all unidentified prey.

5. Colors

dv_palette() gives each name a color and unidentified nodes white. Build it from the names in your own data rather than typing them:

pal <- dv_palette(prep$data$class)
length(pal)
#> [1] 21
head(pal, 6)
#> Malacostraca    Teleostei     Bivalvia  Cephalopoda   Polychaeta Phaeophyceae 
#>    "#1f77b4"    "#aec7e8"    "#ff7f0e"    "#ffbb78"    "#2ca02c"    "#98df8a"

Pass the result to dv_sunburst(colors = pal). To give one taxon a color of your choice, change that element: pal[["Malacostraca"]] <- "#1f77b4". The palette has 20 colors and reuses them after that. With several hundred taxa, as here, dv_palette_tree(tree) is the better choice: one hue per phylum, tints below it.

6. Periods and length classes

Add a covariate column, list it in dv_spec(covariates = ), and build periods and length bins with the helpers:

table(dat$year)
#> 
#> 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 
#>   17   13 3396 2029 3075
dv_add_period(c(2020, 2022, 2023, 2024), breaks = c(2019, 2022, 2024))
#> [1] 2019-2022 2019-2022 2023-2024 2023-2024
#> Levels: 2019-2022 2023-2024
dv_size_bins(c(15, 20, 34, 58), breaks = c(0, 20, 35, 50, 110))
#> [1] [0, 20)   [20, 35)  [20, 35)  [50, 110)
#> Levels: [0, 20) [20, 35) [35, 50) [50, 110)

A year on an inner break goes to the earlier period (2022 above), and a length on an inner break goes to the bin that starts there (20 cm above). Values outside the breaks get no level. The ICES years are very uneven, so choose breaks from the table of years, not from round numbers. The article on covariates shows how to compare diets across the levels.

7. Freshwater, terrestrial and mixed prey

WoRMS covers marine taxa and many brackish and freshwater ones. When DietView matches a name without an ID, it restricts the search to marine records, so a strictly freshwater or terrestrial prey named without an AphiaID will often be unresolved. For such prey, build a lineage table from an authority that covers them (for example GBIF or the Catalogue of Life) and use taxonomy = "table" (section 3). If your prey list mixes marine and other taxa, resolve the marine part with WoRMS, append the rest by hand from the other authority, and say in your methods which authority supplied which part.
